texts: Overview
When: from 12 February 2009
Distance: about 6,300 km (Vancouver ⇔ Yellowknife)
Summary: The far north at −26 °C. A 6,300 km journey across the snow, chasing the aurora in a rented Jeep Grand Cherokee.
Daily record (contents)

toc.title: Arriving in Vancouver and starting the road trip

toc.title: Farewell to the Grand Cherokee, and home

texts: □ Day 1 (12 Feb) Nagoya → Vancouver → Squamish

7:30. We met at the west exit of Nagoya Station. After taking a commemorative photo with the people who came to see us off, we boarded the "Kira Kira" express bus and left Nagoya. The bus stood out with its red body, and inside the seats were roomy and quite comfortable.

Soon after setting off there was a nerve-racking moment. A traffic jam formed on the Tomei Expressway. The worry crossed our minds that we would arrive late and miss our flight. Fortunately the jam soon cleared. The weather was wonderful, and near Gotemba we had a crisp view of a beautifully snow-capped Mt. Fuji.

Just after noon the bus arrived at Tokyo Station. We walked and walked through the huge station to the JR Sobu Line. Our bags were heavy. We changed to the Keiyo Line at Funabashi and reached Narita Airport. The airport is huge too. We went to the Air Canada desk to check in. Here we got our first baptism of English. The automatic check-in machines had no Japanese display, and it took us quite a while. After check-in we dropped our bags and went to the duty-free area. What caught our eye was the TAX FREE AKIHABARA shop, with everything from electronics to rather geeky items.

At last we boarded Air Canada flight 002 and said goodbye to Japan. Apparently it takes about eight and a half hours to Vancouver. It was already dark outside. A while after take-off the in-flight meal came round: seafood curry with bread, salad and cake. The portion was a little small, but the taste was good. You could choose wine as a drink too. After a nap, breakfast was served. I wasn't very hungry. We had crossed the date line, and it was about 7:30 on the 12th, Vancouver time. It felt like we had gained a day. For breakfast you could choose porridge or scrambled eggs. The porridge, by the way, was Western-style.

The plane descended, broke through the low-hanging clouds, and finally land came into view. We passed over Vancouver Island and landed. When we arrived at Vancouver International Airport the weather was dull and overcast. Before getting off we sat in the business-class seats and played around. Business class really is annoyingly comfortable. Inside the airport came a nervous conversation in English at immigration. They asked all sorts of things, but I don't really remember them.

Out of the airport we headed to the Alamo rent-a-car lot. Our partner for this trip: a big red Jeep Grand Cherokee! It had a ski rack on the roof, a spacious and comfortable interior, and even cruise control. We packed in our mountain of luggage and off we went!

First we headed north on Highway 99 toward downtown Vancouver, Canada's third-largest city. In Canada you drive on the right in a left-hand-drive car. At first the difference from Japan felt very strange. Looking at the shops lining the road, we noticed quite a lot of Japanese restaurants. Many of the petrol stations were companies we often see in Japan too, and there was even a 7-Eleven. Canadian traffic lights change quickly. As soon as one turns red it goes back to green. That also means you stop at lights more often.

First we went to a bank called the Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) to change some traveller's cheques into cash. We braved negotiating in English. There turned out to be a lot of paperwork, and we struggled under a barrage of questions we didn't really understand. We were told there would be no fee, but they quietly took $10. Next we went to Mountain Equipment Co-op (MEC), a Canadian outdoor shop, to buy gas canisters. The shop was huge. It had a wide range of everything: tents, sleeping bags, clothes, small items, ski-touring gear and climbing gear. Just walking round the shop was fun.

Having bought seven gas canisters, we set off for lunch. We tried to head to Lonsdale Quay Market in North Vancouver, but on entering downtown Vancouver we were completely thrown about by the roads. Because of one-way streets and elevated roads we just couldn't go in the direction we wanted. We ended up circling BC Place Stadium, the venue for the Olympic opening ceremony, again and again. Then came a fatal mistake. When we finally got out of downtown, we went in completely the opposite direction from the market, and ended up heading along Highway 99 toward Squamish. This road, named the "Sea to Sky Highway", runs along a beautiful coastline toward an inlet. There was no snow at all in Vancouver, but gradually snow began to appear at the roadside. On the left we could see many boats and small islands floating on the sea. It's a pleasant highway, but as the only road to Whistler, an Olympic venue, lane-widening work was going on everywhere. We had lunch at a local café in a village called Lions Bay, a few dozen minutes from Vancouver. We ordered coffee and some unusual sandwiches.

After lunch we continued along the Sea to Sky Highway and reached Squamish, a town exactly halfway between Vancouver and Whistler. It's a fairly large town, with big supermarkets, McDonald's and other shops along Highway 99. The temperature was around 0 °C. First we went to buy ingredients for cooking our own meals. Canadian supermarkets are huge! There were vegetables and canned goods we had never seen in Japan, and we took our time enjoying the shopping. But this shop had no fresh meat or fish counter. A bit disappointing.
□ Day 2 (13 Feb) Squamish ⇔ Whistler (1)

When we woke up, a lovely blue sky had spread out. In the distance we could see pure-white snowy mountains. On the road to Whistler the snow walls at the roadside were big, but the snow clearing was perfect. Again, there was roadwork in several places. There was a fair amount of traffic. Along the Sea to Sky Highway we went from the sea to the mountains. After about an hour of winding road we arrived at Whistler Village.

First we went to the office of a company called Japanada Enterprise to buy lift passes. The receptionist was Japanese, and it was a relief to be able to speak in Japanese. When we said we were going to drive to Yellowknife in a rental car, we were told it was probably impossible. Do even people who live in Canada think driving to Yellowknife in winter is crazy?

We took the Whistler Village Gondola and finally hit the slopes! The Whistler ski area is split across two mountains: Whistler Mountain at 2,182 m and Blackcomb Mountain at 2,440 m. The plan was to ski Whistler on the first day, Blackcomb on the second, and both on the third and fourth. The gondola felt packed and a little cramped, but it's very fast. In no time Whistler Village below became tiny. Getting off the gondola, something was glittering in the air! Diamond dust. The temperature was about −15 °C. The snow was dry, like powder. Kick it and it floats up. A vast ski area spread out, and in the distance we could see snowy mountains continuing on and on. Because it's at a high latitude, about 50° north, at this time of year the sun doesn't rise high even at midday. Even so, the snow on the slopes shone pure white.

After a commemorative photo, we finally started skiing! We enjoyed the best slopes, with powder snow flying up at every turn, and headed for the upper part of Whistler Mountain. The quad lifts were comfortably spaced and fast. As the summit approached, the trees got shorter until we reached the tree line. Above that spread a world of rock and snow. Near the summit there are many cirques called "Bowls", and reasonably advanced skiers can ski down freely from anywhere in the vast Bowl area. The crazy experts are skiing down what are practically cliffs. What's surprising is that these are properly marked on the map and signs as Expert Trails.

You can take a lift right to the summit of Whistler Mountain. From here you get a superb 360° panoramic view. There's also an Inukshuk, a figure of stacked stones that is also the symbol of the Vancouver Olympics. Inukshuks apparently come from Canada's Indigenous peoples. From the summit we skied straight down 1,530 m of vertical to Creekside at the base! The whole run is intermediate, and you can ski at an exhilarating speed. But even for an intermediate run there are mogul slopes here and there. They aren't very steep, so they're good mogul practice, and before long the moguls become fun. A long, varied run: recommended!

Lunch was at a restaurant at the base. We thought the prices were a little high, and ordered one burger each and one salad for the four of us. The result left us dumbfounded. It didn't say it was a set, but each came not only with a giant hamburger but with a huge pile of fries and salad. The salad we shared was heaped on a big plate too, with lots of chicken on top. Of course we ate everything, but we were far too full for skiing. The taste was faultless. We were more than satisfied. Is this the Canadian standard? After lunch we enjoyed the vast slopes of Whistler Mountain again. Skiing above the tree line in particular feels wonderful.

After skiing we toured the supermarkets. We were looking for salmon roe. But neither the supermarket in Whistler Village nor the one in Squamish had any. There were large amounts of many kinds of fresh meat and ham, but few kinds of seafood. Among them we bought fresh salmon and smoked salmon. Tonight's dinner: a double-salmon rice bowl with soy-marinated fresh salmon and grilled smoked salmon! The melting texture and savoury flavour were the best. We also had pumpkin soup and crab-stick salad. The "buttermilk" we used in the soup wasn't ordinary milk but something sour like drinking yoghurt, so the soup turned out sour. An odd taste. By the way, crab sticks are called "Imitation Crab" in English. I didn't expect Canada to have crab sticks too.
□ Day 3 (14 Feb) Squamish ⇔ Whistler (2)

Pizza from the morning today. On a pizza base from the supermarket topped only with cheese and sliced salami, we piled lots of corn and mushrooms and put it in the oven. Baked slowly until browned: a feast of a pizza is ready.

We drove to Whistler. Clear skies again today! At the gondola station it was obvious there were more people than yesterday. Probably because it was Saturday. Today we skied Blackcomb Mountain all day. First we took the Blackcomb Excalibur Gondola. Compared with Whistler, Blackcomb has more steep slopes and more mogul runs. Halfway up there are a great many intermediate and advanced runs, each with its own character, from steep runs where you pick up speed to mogul courses covered in bumps, and it's fun. There are several park courses of different difficulty with jumps and a huge halfpipe. Taking the Glacier Express quad lift brings you straight out above the tree line into a silver-white world. The ski area really is vast. There are so many people that the lift queues stretch out, but skiing the runs there's no cramped feeling of nearly colliding with others, and the freedom to ski wherever you like feels great.

You can't reach the summit of Blackcomb at 2,440 m, but you can reach the highest point of the ski area at 2,240 m on a lift called the "Showcase T-Bar". It's an unusual lift: a bar shaped like an upside-down T hangs from the cable, and two people sit against the bar and hold on, sliding up the slope. Your skis or board stay on the snow. For first-timers this is quite tricky. Shinoda and Horibe fell off the lift twice.

Getting off the Showcase T-Bar, a glacier slope called the Horstman Glacier spreads out on the right, but for some reason many other people didn't go that way; they took off their skis and climbed the slope in front. Curious, we climbed the slope for a while too, and an enormous, breathtaking glacier slope appeared on the left. This is the Blackcomb Glacier, which is also designated a provincial park. It's rated intermediate, and there is a groomed run between flags, but for this huge glacier that's no more than a single thin line. In fact few people were skiing the groomed part; everyone was skiing wherever they liked. The snow quality was of course the best. But in places rocks were exposed, so you have to be careful. After enjoying a long run on the glacier, the run leads straight into a forest run. This run was long and fun too.

Next we went to a silver-white area called "7th Heaven", which spreads out from the top of a lift called the "Horstman T-Bar". This is a vast area too, but the groomed runs are clearly marked, and there are gentle beginner runs as well. Of course there are plenty of intermediate and advanced runs: the intermediate "Hugh's Heaven" and "Panorama" let you fly over the best snow at top speed, while the advanced "Sunburn" and "Angel Dust" are covered in moguls. Riding the 7th Heaven Express lets you enjoy them again and again efficiently.

We decided to have lunch at the "Horstman Hut" restaurant at the top of 7th Heaven. You can eat on the outdoor terrace, and the view from here is very good. The location is the best; the drawback is that it's a bit pricey. A normal meal easily goes over $15.

After lunch, while skiing in 7th Heaven, there was an accident! Naoto hit his lower back on a rock and was injured. At this point Naoto had to leave the slopes. While the remaining three were skiing, this time Horibe took a big fall on a steep mogul slope! The impact twisted a part of his binding 90 degrees, and it wouldn't go back no matter how hard he tried. But when he took the ski to the hut at the top of the lift and explained in broken English, a staff member fixed it by banging on it with a hammer.

After this we took on the mogul slope halfway up and then came down. Back in Squamish we went to a big supermarket called "Save-On-Foods". It was fun, with a wide range of products like pasta and sweets sold by weight. There was a wide variety of fresh food like vegetables and meat too. For dinner we made and ate beef stew.
□ Day 4 (15 Feb) Squamish ⇔ Whistler (3)

Breakfast was frozen spring rolls and cheese meat pies, chicken soup with shell pasta, and so on. It was supposed to come with potato salad and juice, but they had vanished from the fridge where we'd put them! Even though we'd written our names on them. Probably another guest took them. A shame.

Today we would ski both Whistler and Blackcomb. Naoto rested in Whistler Village. The weather was perfect again today. Diamond dust was sparkling too. As it was Sunday there were lots of people. First, Whistler Mountain. With three of us, many people rode the lift with us. Canadians chat to you quite casually even when they know you're Japanese. We could more or less understand most of it, and reply in broken English. A lot of it was "Where are you from?" or "Japanese food is great", but at one point a funny Canadian got on our lift. At first he talked about the usual things, but gradually he started firing off dirty jokes. Not that we understood English dirty jokes. We knew they were dirty jokes because of the big gestures around his crotch. He said he was 41, and he was a really funny guy.

We skied the runs we hadn't covered on the first day. "Staccato Glades", a tree run where you weave between countless trees growing on a bumpy slope, demands quick turns, and it's thrilling and fun. The advanced "Dave Murray Downhill", used for the Olympic alpine skiing events, is a superb run: steep with no moguls all the way. We picked up so much speed that the only way to control it was to fall. It has apparently been used as a World Cup course many times.

There were still many runs we hadn't skied, but from midday we rode the "PEAK 2 PEAK" gondola, newly completed in 2008, spanning 4.4 km between Whistler and Blackcomb, over to Blackcomb. There are only four towers between the gondola stations. It passes more than 400 m above the valley between the two mountains. The unsupported span is 3.024 km, said to be the longest in the world. Far below we could see Whistler Village, a completely frozen lake and even the Sea to Sky Highway.

Arriving at Blackcomb, we visited the Blackcomb Glacier we had enjoyed yesterday once more. This time we aimed for the parts we hadn't skied yesterday. Even coming two days in a row, this glacier has a grandeur that moves you just as much. After that we enjoyed all sorts of runs and charged into the park with its jumps. Features in this park are marked S, M or L by difficulty. The jumps marked "L" are enormous, and watching boarders launch big airs and spin in the air left our jaws hanging. Meanwhile we charged at the "M" jumps! Sometimes it went well, sometimes it hurt... Horibe even tried the halfpipe on skis.

Back home in Squamish. Tonight's dinner was a Special Menu! We had bought a whole big lobster at the supermarket. As we roasted the lobster whole in the oven, its dark colour turned bright red. Once it was done we split it down the back in one stroke. The tail was packed with meat. The meat was really plump, and dipped in butter it was incredibly good!! We cracked the claws and ate the meat inside too. The other dish was okonomiyaki with bacon. Because we used red cabbage, the whole thing was purple. We seasoned it with consommé, but it turned out surprisingly Japanese-tasting. When eating it we tried salt and pepper, a knob of butter, and maple syrup.
□ Day 5 (16 Feb) Squamish ⇔ Whistler (4)

This morning's breakfast was a typical Canadian family breakfast? I don't know if it is, but: cereal with milk, lettuce and cauliflower salad, and fruit with yoghurt. The red cabbage left over from yesterday's okonomiyaki came out shredded, but raw it was a bit... Very unpopular.

Today was our last day at Whistler. Clear skies. Sunny all four days, it's hard to believe. There seems to be no rain-bringer in this group. I'm a bit worried for the other group. To make the most of our last Whistler day, the snowboarders Naoto and Shinoda went to Blackcomb, and the skiers KEN and Horibe went to Whistler. We expected fewer people since it was Monday, but that wasn't the case. At 9:00 there was a huge queue at the gondola, a 25-minute wait. And for some reason there seemed to be lots of children.

The skiers headed for a huge cirque on Whistler Mountain, "Rhapsody Bowl". Around here the lifts and runs all have musical names: "Symphony Express", "Harmony Express", "Adagio", "Flute Bowl" and so on. This area seems to have especially good snow and fewer people, a bit of a hidden gem. It's certainly a long way from the top of the gondola, somewhere you can only reach by checking the map carefully and changing lifts. On top of that, the entrance to Rhapsody Bowl is hard to find. When we finally reached the top of Rhapsody Bowl, there was almost nobody there, and a vast snow-covered cirque spread all the way round. Unlike the Blackcomb Glacier, set between towering rock walls, this cirque spreads out in gentle, beautiful curves. For a while we were so moved by its beauty that we couldn't start skiing straight away. First we traversed across the slope and moved to a spot few people had skied. From there we skied straight down to the bottom. The snow was very soft. It flew up easily and our bodies were wrapped in powder. It isn't groomed at all, so it's a bit bumpy. And here came another accident. Horibe fell where the snow rose up and hit his elbow hard. For now we decided to wait and see, and took a lunch break.

Lunch was at a restaurant on the mountain. Starting to miss Japanese food, we ordered the "Japanese Miso Soup Noodle" and a sushi roll called the "Dynamite Roll". The miso soup noodles weren't like miso ramen; they were ramen in a purely Japanese miso soup, with tofu and bean sprouts. The Dynamite Roll is a prawn tempura roll with avocado. The seaweed is rolled inside. It tasted nostalgic. Canadian restaurants mostly serve sandwiches and burgers full of cheese and meat. But Japanese food has definitely taken root in Canada. Many of the other Canadian customers seemed to be eating noodles and rice bowls skilfully with chopsticks. We rested for a while after eating, but Horibe's elbow pain didn't ease much, so the skiers came down here.

The two skiers decided to wander around Whistler Village until the snowboarders came down. We strolled about buying souvenirs. Then we found "Sushi Village", a sushi restaurant a Canadian on the lift had told us was good. But it wasn't open yet.

After meeting up we went round the shops in the village and went back to Squamish. As an end-of-skiing celebration we bought some alcohol today. In Canada the law says you have to be 19 or over to drink. Dinner was seafood pasta. Oysters, mussels and clams sautéed with vegetables and butter, on top of pasta. Thanks to a huge amount of pasta someone else in the kitchen gave us, saying "We had too much", it was a mega portion. We drank wine and liqueur cider too, and filled both our stomachs and our hearts. I think we'll sleep well tonight.
□ Day 6 (17 Feb) Squamish → Jasper

At last the time came to leave our familiar lodging in Squamish. After five nights, leaving felt a little sad. We didn't have much time today, so breakfast was McDonald's. When Naoto ordered an Egg McMuffin set, sets for all four of us arrived. McDonald's seemed much the same as in Japan in size and taste.

From Squamish we drove north along Highway 99, past Whistler. The snowy mountains in the morning sun were beautiful. From here the road was new to us. After Pemberton, a village with many ranches, the road narrowed, the surface got worse and it became a twisting mountain road. The rivers were frozen, covered in snow and pure white. Even so, the snow had been properly cleared from the road. But signs saying "Avalanche Area" stood here and there, and slopes that looked ready to shed rocks at any moment towered over the roadside with no protection at all. Driving through these wild mountains, we came across a beautiful, completely frozen lake. The rime ice around it was superb too. We stopped here for photos. The thermometer showed −15 °C.

Coming down the tough mountain road, which had hairpin bends too, we came out at the town of Lillooet. There was less snow around here. Lillooet is where the river has eroded the reddish-brown bedrock into a large, deep valley. From here the road follows gentle hills on the river terraces along the valley. Cattle and horses grazed here and there, and vast snow-covered farms appeared, but they were concentrated around the settlements. Between settlements, tens of kilometres apart, untouched wilderness stretched on with nothing but the road. We stopped to refuel at a station in the town of Cache Creek. Canadian petrol stations always have a shop like a convenience store, and you pay for fuel at its counter.

From Cache Creek we joined Highway 1, the "Trans-Canada Highway" that crosses the continent from east to west. From here it's a fast road with a 100 km/h limit. Using the Grand Cherokee's cruise control, we left the speed to the car. We drove on and on, alternating between snow-covered wilderness and small settlements, and when a big river called the Thompson River came into view, the city of Kamloops was near.

Kamloops is one of the larger towns in British Columbia. We thought we'd have lunch there... but Highway 1 bypasses the town without going in. We carried straight on onto Highway 5, the Yellowhead Highway, which continues to today's destination, Jasper. Checking the map, there weren't many towns ahead that looked likely to have restaurants. We often passed settlements on the map with fewer than 500 people without even noticing. Just as we were getting really hungry, we found a burger shop called A&W in a town called Clearwater! A&W seems to be a very major fast-food chain in Canada. The burgers have family names like "Mama Burger" and "Uncle Burger". The Uncle Burger has a thick sirloin patty and is very filling. We reckoned it was bigger than McDonald's too. Shinoda's "Grandpa Burger" was three thick patties stacked up. One was more than enough at Canadian portions.

We continued along Highway 5, looking at beautiful mountains designated as a provincial park. It had been cloudy for a while, but gradually the sun came out and the snowy mountains began to shine. By the time we'd driven all this way it was already evening. The Yellowhead Highway changes from Highway 5 to Highway 16. From here is Mount Robson Provincial Park. Ahead of the road, Mt. Robson, the highest peak in the Canadian Rockies at 3,954 m, came into view, towering majestically. It is triangular, with distinctive horizontal stripes of snow and rock. And then, at last, we crossed the Rockies. Crossing the long Rocky Mountains, we had imagined a steep mountain road. But the speed limit stayed at 90–100 km/h. Almost flat, straight road continued all the way. Just as we were thinking something was odd, we crossed the Yellowhead Pass and a sign marking the Alberta border appeared. Crossing the Rockies was so easy it was an anticlimax. There was no snow on the road either, though we had been wondering whether our all-season tyres would be OK.

By the time we reached the town of Jasper it was already dark. In the quiet, deserted forest of Jasper National Park, it was a relief to see the lights of the town. After refuelling, we went to look for tonight's lodging, Jasper International Hostel. But when we went to the place we had looked up, there was no hostel. When we asked a local, they said it was out of town at the foot of the mountains to the south. Checking the map again, it was certainly there. But it was far from here, so we decided to have dinner first. We went into a nearby pizza place and ordered one 12-inch pizza for all of us. Freshly baked and loaded with toppings, it was delicious.

Leaving town and heading south up a pitch-dark mountain road, we finally found the hostel and checked in. As a youth hostel, the bedroom was just a big room lined with bunk beds. And the beds didn't even have curtains. As it was winter there were few other guests, but in summer it's apparently popular and fills up with bookings quickly. You couldn't relax in a place like this, and we worried about our luggage too. So we went into Jasper again. We drove around the little town, decorated with snow and illuminations. There were a great many hotels. But it was late, so most shops were closed. After enjoying the atmosphere of Jasper, we went into a convenience-type shop that was still open, bought snacks and tomorrow's breakfast, and went back to the hostel.
□ Day 7 (18 Feb) Jasper → High Level

Early in the morning, while the room was still quiet, we got up and gathered in the kitchen. Another long drive today. We quickly ate cereal, savoury bread, salad and so on, and left before sunrise. The temperature outside was −13 °C. Being a town in the Rockies, it really was cold.

After driving for a while the sun slowly rose. The sunrise and the Rocky Mountains made a magical atmosphere. The road was almost straight, with no snow left on the surface, and easy to drive. A fast road with a limit of mostly 100 km/h went on. We kept looking around the roadside in case wildlife like elk or moose appeared, but sadly we didn't see any. Going straight on along Highway 16 would take us directly to Edmonton, but after leaving the national park we turned left onto Highway 40. On this stretch there are no petrol stations for over 100 km. We drove on and on through gentle hills where nobody lives at all. Oncoming cars came only occasionally. Moving away from the Rockies, there are hardly any high mountains. For how cold it was, there wasn't much snow. We could see the road stretching far into the distance through the forest that covers the land.

Past the town of Grande Cache, as we came to the city of Grande Prairie, a plain so vast you could see the horizon spread out. Grande Prairie is a fair-sized city, and for the first time today we were stopped at a traffic light. Leaving the city for the outskirts, vast farms filled the plain. With no trees, the snow had piled up and everything was pure white to the horizon. Under a blue sky we headed north along a dead-straight road across the silver-white plateau.

We crossed the great frozen Peace River and stopped for lunch in a small town called Grimshaw. The restaurant we went into was called Sammy's. Burgers were the main thing, but there were some distinctive dishes. Naoto ordered the "3 Cheese Calzone": three kinds of cheese wrapped in dough and baked. He raved about it. KEN ordered the "Chicken Supreme": fried chicken and fries topped with melted cheese and thick gravy, and the gravy was the best.

With full stomachs, we resumed our crossing of the continent. About 300 km to our destination, High Level. On this stretch there is only one town with more than 1,000 people. The northern half of Alberta has a very low population density; most people are concentrated in cities in the southern half like Edmonton and Calgary. Heading ever north on a single road through the forest, settlements and snow-covered fields and ranches appeared here and there. There were hardly any junctions either. When we stopped to change drivers at a settlement called Twin Lake, a dog came out of a house, so we played with it. It's amazing how lively dogs are even somewhere this cold.

Just before High Level, we spotted something lying on the left side of the road. Stopping the car and going closer, we found a dead deer-like animal. Was it hit by a car? After this, we saw the same kind of thing twice more.

We arrived in High Level, a town of about 4,000 people. Restaurants and lodgings line the main street. Tonight we stayed at the "Best Canadian Motor Inn". A motor inn (motel) is lodging for people travelling by car, and there are lots of them along Canada's main roads. But today too the location we had looked up was wrong, and we had to ask a local. When we checked in, the room had two plush double beds, was quite spacious and comfortable. It even had a TV, fridge, microwave and coffee maker, and of course a bathroom. Wireless LAN was free too. All this for just over 100 dollars a room is cheap! For four people it's a great deal.

Dinner was at a nearby Chinese restaurant. Chinese food for the first time in a while. But the fried spring rolls were cinnamon-flavoured, and the sauce on the fried chicken balls was apple jam of all things. Chinese food in Canada is interesting. We also stopped at a supermarket and bought a chocolate cake on sale at half price. We ate it in our room. So full!

At night light snow started to fall. Our first snow since coming to Canada. It was so cold that it didn't melt at all when it hit the ground. After a while everything was white. The Jeep was covered in snow too.
□ Day 8 (19 Feb) High Level → Yellowknife

This motel offers a free breakfast. The self-service spread had bread, cereal, muffins, yoghurt, apples, waffles, French toast, and drinks like coffee and milk. We gratefully ate all sorts of things. And it seems we ate too much.

Today's destination was Yellowknife. High Level is at 58° north; Yellowknife is at 62°. The border between Alberta and the Northwest Territories is at 60°. For reference, Cape Soya, the northernmost point of Japan, is at 45°. The snow seemed to have stopped during the night, but the road was white and the centre line was completely invisible. A little worried, we set off for Yellowknife. But there was no sense of the tyres slipping at all. There wasn't much traffic, but when an oncoming car passed, the snow on the road flew up and was blown to the shoulder, clearing the road naturally. When a big vehicle like a truck came the other way, the huge amount of snow it kicked up turned our view white and we couldn't see anything for a moment, which was quite frightening. Around here the scenery hardly changes no matter how far you go; you just keep going along a single wide white road through the forest.

Just before noon we finally reached 60° north, the border of the Northwest Territories (NWT). There's a big sign marking the border. From here we drove the Mackenzie Highway, NWT Highway 1. In Enterprise, the first small town we found after entering the Northwest Territories, we refuelled and bought lunch. There didn't seem to be any restaurants, just a small petrol station and a shop.

Highway 1 was snow-covered in places, but it wasn't that bad a road. Coniferous forest stretched along both sides the whole way. At the junction of Highway 1 and Highway 3 (the Yellowknife Highway) we took Highway 3, and after a while we finally reached the ice road across the Mackenzie River. There is still no bridge across this river; in summer cars cross by ferry, and in winter they drive on the ice. When the ice is melting and when it is starting to form, traffic is cut off. A sign before the river said that vehicles of up to 64,000 kg could currently cross.

Out on the ice road, a pure white world spread out with the Mackenzie River on the left and Great Slave Lake on the left. Only the ice surface where cars pass was tinted a pale earth colour. Great Slave Lake, the tenth largest lake in the world, looked as if it spread beyond the horizon. And for some reason there were lots of ravens. They clustered around the car.

From here to Yellowknife is about 300 km. In between there isn't a single settlement along the road. There's no mobile signal either, so if something happened it would be very troublesome. And this area seems to be a bison warning zone. There were lots of bison warning signs. The trees beside the road were getting shorter, and there were occasional open views. The temperature at midday was −21 °C.

Buildings suddenly appeared out of the untamed wilderness. Then road signs abruptly multiplied and we plunged into the centre of Yellowknife. It all happened in an instant. It really felt like a city. To think high-rise buildings stand in a place this far north... At −20 °C the city was full of life, with many people walking about. We checked in to a motel called "Arnica Inn", a little past the centre. It had recently been renovated, and the rooms were clean and comfortable. And this place was cheap too. We couldn't completely understand the English conversation with the receptionist, but we got to stay for less than the price we had looked up.

We walked out for dinner. It really was cold. You could feel the inside of your nostrils freezing. The temperature on the city's electronic sign showed −24 °C. Cold enough that even mobile phone screens went strange. It's amazing that so many people were still walking about.

We ended up at a sushi restaurant called "Sushi North". The staff were all Japanese. We chatted with them about our trip so far and ordered a nigiri set. What they especially recommended was Arctic char nigiri. Apparently you can only eat it here. It had a texture like toro, melting in an instant in your mouth and spreading a rich flavour. There was also salmon, tuna and prawn nigiri, plus a Dynamite roll and a California roll. We all left very satisfied, and the temperature had dropped to −26 °C.

Back at the motel, we relaxed, and late at night we went outside and looked up at the sky. Some cloud had spread. The city lights got in the way too, and it looked like we wouldn't see the aurora today. But after a while we went out again. Looking from a place away from the city lights, we could tell there was a faint aurora. We would see it properly tomorrow.
□ Day 9 (20 Feb) Yellowknife (stay)

Today we were joining a dog-sledding experience from midday. Until then, free time. KEN and Naoto got going from the morning. Shinoda and Horibe slept soundly in the room until just before noon. Breakfast was the free self-service, as the day before.

After eating we explored the town. It was cold, so we wore our ski wear. The shops weren't open yet, so we headed for the outskirts. There was an ice road on Great Slave Lake here too. Walking along the ice road, there were houses built on the ice. Looking closely, their bases were like rafts, with rubber tyres fixed around them. In summer the houses must float on the lake, moored to the shore.
Next we went up a small hill. There's a monument, and it's a perfect place to look out over Yellowknife. We could clearly see the ice road continuing far into the distance.

We walked into town and looked around galleries and shopping malls. Yellowknife once prospered from gold mining, and now prospers from diamond mining. So there were diamond counters in several places. But of course they were expensive.

After each of us had lunch, we took a bus for the dog-sledding tour. All of the 30 or so participants were Japanese, and so was the guide. Everyone must have flown in; nobody else would have come by car. Aurora Village was in the forest about 30 minutes out of town. Tonight's aurora viewing would be at the same place. Lots of dogs were kept there, barking non-stop. Ten dogs pull a sled, and they seemed to be barking to make the case that they should be the ones pulling. Once the first sled run had left, the dogs that had been barking so much suddenly fell silent. Then when the sled came back they started barking furiously again.

We got on the second run. The dogs pulling were the same as on the first run, and a local Indigenous musher rode on the back of the sled to control it. Weren't they tired? The dogs were very strong. The sled went faster than we expected. Over bumps the sled even bounced up. This momentum was great fun. On uphills they paused, then pushed up through sheer guts. When we stopped once, one dog even had a pee. On downhills it was so fast it felt like flying. A precious experience.

After the dog sled we went to the campfire and toasted marshmallows. If you toast a marshmallow carefully without burning it, the outside turns golden brown, crisp outside and gooey inside, and it's delicious.

Next we enjoyed the tube slide. You climb a big snow slide, get into a tube and slide down. You pick up more speed than you'd expect. Not satisfied with sliding alone, we tried linking all four of us together and sliding down at once. But the person in front went down with too much force, and the back always broke away; it was quite hard. When we finally succeeded after many tries, it felt great.
We also got to try walking on the snow in snowshoes. A first for us, and quite tricky. On slopes we sometimes went flying.

Back in town, we went to the information centre and got certificates for crossing 60° north. They're quite proper certificates. In front of the information centre a flock of pure-white ptarmigans had gathered.

We agreed that we wanted to eat bison meat for dinner, and headed to "Bullocks' Bistro", which we had been told served that kind of meat. It's a small place, but inside there were signatures written all over, and it did seem like a top restaurant. There was no bison that day, but there was caribou and other dishes using unusual ingredients on the menu. But, but, it was far too expensive! Around 30 dollars a dish. And the menu said to pay a 20% tip. We ordered a few dishes at first, but the lady running the place told us each person had to order one dish. When we said it was too expensive to order, she said "Go to McDonald's then", and we left.
The next restaurant we went to was a place combined with a bar, reasonably priced, and everyone ordered what they liked, such as pizza and pasta.

Then at night we took the bus back to Aurora Village. There were huge numbers of Japanese people who had come to see the aurora; apparently about 150 had come. First a Japanese staff member explained all the facilities of Aurora Village. We couldn't really tell, but apparently the aurora was already out, if weak. They said that with a high-performance camera it would show up green. Until the aurora got stronger, we could warm up in tents of the Indigenous peoples called tipis. But tonight it wasn't that cold, apparently only around −10 °C. Yesterday had been colder. As a late-night snack we were given bison soup and bread. Good thing we didn't force ourselves to go and eat bison meat. The soup was full of ingredients, with proper chunks of meat. On the bread we spread maple margarine, a mix of maple syrup and margarine, which is quite good. We decided to spread lots on.

After the snack, we gazed at the night sky from a hill with a good view. Then in the north-east, a light that at first was only faintly visible gradually grew stronger. Cheers went up. Band-like light from green to white swayed, swirled and moved. Gradually the bands of aurora spread right overhead too, and we could see them changing shape. The mysterious light kept growing stronger and weaker, and held our eyes fixed. At that moment we even forgot how cold it was. We heard later that the aurora level that night was 4 on a scale of 5. Until the day before, the weather had been poor and the aurora had hardly been visible, so we were lucky to see a level 4. We didn't see one this time, but apparently a level 5 aurora "explodes".

After returning to the motel, we got in the Jeep and went to the ice road to see the aurora again. Drive 5 km out of town on the ice road and the city lights become much weaker. We saw the aurora. We couldn't see light as strong as earlier, but we could observe light that was moving.
□ Day 10 (21 Feb) Yellowknife → High Level

We had a breakfast of bread and cereal at the motel and left. From here to High Level there are almost no places to eat lunch, so we bought it in advance at McDonald's in Yellowknife. Today we went back along the road we came by. No refuelling for over 300 km. We may have been getting a bit bored of the unchanging road with no towns or anything.

We crossed the Mackenzie River, and up to here all was well. But just before the town of Enterprise, there was an accident. It was at a point where a similar long straight changed into a gentle right-hand curve. There had been no oncoming cars for a while. The speed was set by cruise control, with no need to adjust it. The driver must have dozed off for a moment. When we noticed, the right wheels had slid down the slope of the shoulder and the car couldn't be controlled. He stamped desperately on the brake, but the car ploughed into the snow wall at the roadside. When the car stopped, the bumper had broken off. Reversing just spun the wheels and we couldn't get out. Then a car stopped for us and towed us back onto the road with a rope. We were saved. And the car moved. But the radiator had been damaged, and coolant seemed to be leaking. We bought coolant at the shop in Enterprise. When we somehow reached the motel in High Level, we were truly relieved.
Dinner was KFC. We ordered the 15-piece Barrel set. It was just the right amount for four.
□ Day 11 (22 Feb) High Level → Manning

After the same free breakfast as on the morning of day 8, we checked on the Jeep we had crashed yesterday. The coolant seemed to have stopped leaking. Or rather, the area around the radiator was frozen solid. When we tried the engine it started first time, but we thought we heard a slight odd noise. We set off for now. At first it seemed fine.

The car was towed to Manning Collision Repair, a collision repair company. To continue our trip, we had to reach Vancouver in this car no matter what. The repair staff were keen to fix it, but said it would take about a week. That would mean we couldn't go back to Japan, so we started negotiating, with the company's boss joining in. Our English was poor, so we negotiated with help from the simultaneous interpreting of Sompo Japan's overseas support service. We also needed a decision from the rental company, Alamo, so the interpreter was simultaneously interpreting between the repair company, Alamo and Naoto. After long negotiations, they agreed to repair it just enough for the car to run. But today was Sunday, so the repairs would start tomorrow. The boss told us to bring the car to the workshop tomorrow morning, so we decided to stay in Manning tonight.

We decided to stay at the Manning Motor Inn, a motel similar to the one in High Level. But it was 11:30 at the time. We wondered if we could check in at this hour, but it was OK. We had lunch at the café in the motel. We ordered one big platter. The amount was just right for four, but it was mostly fried food and felt a bit heavy.

There wasn't much to do in the room, so we passed the time napping, playing cards, reading books and so on. When we turned on the TV, curling was on. It seemed to be a Canadian inter-provincial championship. Even if we couldn't understand a word of the English, sport is universal. Curling is something we only watch during the Olympics, but it was fun to watch.

Maybe because lunch was heavy, or because we'd just been lying around, we didn't get very hungry even in the evening. At around 8 o'clock we all went to a convenience store, bought sandwiches and other light snacks, and made do with those tonight.
□ Day 12 (23 Feb) Manning (stay)

This motel's breakfast wasn't free. A bit of a shame. We ordered the breakfast set at the café where we had lunch yesterday. Reasonably priced, generous and good value. Only Horibe, who didn't order the set, got just a single French toast for about the same price.

Around 8 o'clock we took the car to the workshop. It seemed fine for short drives. We met the boss and handed him a letter we had written yesterday. Afterwards he asked us to come back tomorrow morning, and we left the workshop.

With a whole day free, we decided to explore the town of Manning. The town was covered in snow, and the river crossing the centre was completely frozen. The sign showed −18 °C. It was cold, so we went into a nearby supermarket and a general store and browsed slowly. For lunch we bought bread, salad and so on at the supermarket. It's a small town, but the supermarket was very big.
After that, relaxing time in the room. Like yesterday, we spent the whole time lazing about until night.
□ Day 13 (24 Feb) Manning → Edmonton

Light snow was falling, but the powder on the road was blown away by the wind and the draught of passing cars. We drove on south, driving safely. The great plain continued, but at the town of Peace River we crossed a big valley along the river on a bridge.

We passed through Peace River and just after 2 p.m. went into Sammy's restaurant in a small town called Valleyview. It seemed to be the same chain as the one in Grimshaw on day 7. We ate burgers and salads, and again they were original dishes we had never had before, and we were satisfied. The photo is a hamburger with mushroom gratin sauce.

Valleyview is where highways meet. From here we took Highway 43. What's different about this highway from those we had driven so far is that almost the whole way has a median. Not a row of blocks like in Japan, but a wide ditch tens of metres across. Something only possible in a country as big as Canada. By the way, on the sections with this wide median the limit is 110 km/h.

As Edmonton approached, we gradually passed one big town after another. It was getting quite dark, and the lights of the city at night began to stand out. At last we entered the city of Edmonton. The roads run north–south in a grid. Light snow kept falling; the main roads were perfectly cleared, but narrow side streets were white. The city is probably too big to clear every little street. When stopping at lights and so on, the ABS sometimes kicked in where the snow hadn't been cleared.

We found the Days Inn we had looked up online and checked in. Unlike the motels so far with big car parks, it had rooftop parking. But even in a city, it was only 110 dollars a room (about 8,500 yen at the time)! The rooms were big and the beds were plush. Two of us share a double bed, but in Canada travelling as four is the way to go.

Tonight again we wandered the city looking for a place to eat. Our target was genuine Alberta beef. We asked the person in the hotel lobby about steak restaurants, but couldn't find one. As we kept wandering in the light snow, we were drawn to one place: "Japanese Village". The sign said teppanyaki dining. When we went in, some kind of party was going on in a dark room. There didn't seem to be any ordinary customers. We thought we had come to the wrong place, but a staff member came out from the back to greet us and handed us menus. Sure enough, the menu had steak! When we asked, they said they used Alberta beef. We ordered straight away.

We ordered two New York steaks (10 oz, about 280 g) and two tenderloin steaks. Both were top-grade AAA Alberta beef. In front of our table was a big iron griddle. Here a chef with tattoos on his arms appeared at the griddle. First he asked how we wanted our meat cooked. When he realised we were Japanese, he brought over a Japanese staff member, who explained for us. After the explanation, soup, salad and rice came first. The chef began with an advanced performance, holding knives in both hands, clanging them on the griddle and spinning them deftly like juggling. Then, keeping up the performance, he elegantly started grilling onion, zucchini, mushrooms and prawns. Even cutting with the knife was part of the show. When they were nicely done, he divided them onto our four plates. The prawns were plump and incredibly tasty. Next he put the big sirloin (New York steak) and tenderloin on the griddle and started grilling. Meanwhile the chef also began stir-frying bean sprouts in butter on the griddle, skilfully using a knife in each hand. He even made a heart shape out of the bean sprouts. The meat had developed a nice brown crust. Here he put a green butter on the meat and cut it into cubes. The steak, cooked medium, arrived on our plates. Put the sirloin in your mouth and the rich fat floods out and it seems to melt. The tenderloin (fillet) is so tender the fibres come apart in an instant. Both were simply the best. And the sauce was great too: a house-made sesame sauce whose deep richness went perfectly with the meat. Just pouring the sauce over rice made the rice disappear. The course finished with ice cream for dessert. Not just the meat, but the vegetables and soup were all delicious too. The price was about $120 plus tip for four, but for a steak course this generous with the chef's performance, I think it's a real bargain. After the meal, we also enjoyed chatting with the Japanese woman on staff about our trip so far. She said she had come to Canada on a working holiday. This restaurant we found by chance is without doubt the No. 1 of this trip.
□ Day 14 (25 Feb) Edmonton → Radium Hot Springs

Today's schedule was long, so we got up early and left without breakfast. The original plan was to spend a night in Calgary and head straight to Vancouver the next day, but we changed the plan: today we would go to the Rockies, drive the Icefields Parkway, visit the Columbia Icefield and bathe in the hot springs at Radium Hot Springs. Nearly 900 km, quite a hard distance.

The morning temperature was −18 °C. Colder than expected, and snowing too. But once in the car the cold was no problem. We meant to head south from Edmonton, but the city roads were complicated and we struggled to get out. I think we took quite a long detour. Finally we got out to the suburbs and, a little further on, entered the oil town of Leduc. We decided to buy breakfast at the drive-through of a fast-food chain called "Tim Hortons" in Leduc. But we couldn't place four detailed orders, so we all got the same set: a mixed berry muffin, an egg salad sandwich and juice. It was quite good and we liked it.

From Leduc we continued south on the divided highway. Looking at the map before the city of Red Deer, we found a road from here to the Rockies without going all the way to Calgary. This was clearly shorter. Changing plans, we switched to Highway 11, heading west from Red Deer. There wasn't much traffic, but along the way the town of Sylvan Lake, with its beautiful frozen lake, and the town of Rocky Mountain House at the foot of the Rockies were lively and worth seeing.

From Rocky Mountain House there are no petrol stations at all. Hardly any other cars used the road toward the Rockies, and the further we went, the more snow there was on the road. At the national park gate before the Icefields Parkway, the snow had hardly been cleared and was deep on the road. We slowed right down. By the way, at this time of year there's nobody at the gate. Once through the gate and out on the Icefields Parkway, the snow had been cleared to some extent. Even so, there were white stretches of road here and there, so we couldn't let our guard down.

We drove the Icefields Parkway toward Jasper (north-west), heading for the Columbia Icefield. Rugged snowy mountains and rock walls seemed to close in on both sides of the road. Driving carefully along the winding road, a car park and a lodge appeared. But they are closed at this time of year. The trail to the Columbia Icefield was also shut by deep snow. It was snowing, so we couldn't see its whole extent even from a distance, which was a bit disappointing.

Next we turned back the way we came and headed for Lake Louise. It's a small town of fewer than 1,000 people, but it has Lake Louise, so beautiful it's called "the jewel of the Rockies", and in summer tourists flock here. In winter too there's the Lake Louise ski area nearby with over 100 runs, so we thought it might be lively like Whistler, but the snow-covered town was quiet. We had lunch at a restaurant, and there were no other customers at all.

After Lake Louise, we headed for Banff on Highway 1. On the way the cloud thinned and we could see "Castle Mountain", a mountain shaped like a castle. It has a row of sharp rocky peaks and really does look like castle walls.

Rounding Castle Mountain, we arrived in Banff. Lots of people were walking around carrying skis and snowboards. There are many famous large ski areas near Banff. But we had almost no time this trip, so we just quickly went round the highlights. First we went to the front of "The Fairmont Banff Springs", a magnificent top-class hotel in the style of an old castle. After that, about 20 minutes of free time. In winter there are fewer people than in summer, so many shops seemed to have discount sales on souvenirs. There was also a souvenir shop called the OK Gift Shop, owned by Kyosen Ohashi.

Leaving Banff, we drove the Bow Valley Parkway, a winding road through the forest, and from Lake Louise came down out of the Rockies. It gradually got dark, and we carefully descended the snowy downhill road. "Radium Hot Springs" is the name of the hot spring and also of the town around it. When we arrived at Radium Hot Springs it was about 7:30 p.m. and pitch dark. The hot springs are split into a pool type with slightly cooler water and a bath type with hotter water, both mixed open-air baths. You have to wear a swimsuit, though. Even at this hour it was busy with lots of people, young and old. The hot-spring pool is big enough to swim around in. Naoto, well prepared, had brought goggles. The hot bath is small, full with ten people, but at a pleasant temperature, and it washed away the tiredness of the trip. What bothered us was that quite a strong smell of chlorine lingered. It felt more like a pool than a hot spring.

We still hadn't found a place to stay tonight. Fortunately there were several motels, so we were able to check in somewhere decent. Only 85 dollars a room. Far too cheap. But for dinner, it was past nine, and we couldn't find anywhere open. What we found was a small restaurant inside the shop of a Husky petrol station. We could eat at a reasonable price.
□ Day 15 (26 Feb) Radium Hot Springs → Vancouver
Breakfast at the Husky restaurant while it was still dark. The sausages were extra thick.

The trip was finally reaching its climax. The last long drive, toward Vancouver. In the morning it was cloudy, but it gradually cleared and the beautiful snowy mountains of British Columbia came into view. We drove along the gentle foothills of the Rockies to a town called Golden, and from here took Trans-Canada Highway 1 over the Columbia Mountains. On the way we also passed through Glacier National Park. Snowy mountains holding glaciers loomed right in front of us; a very beautiful place.

Passing along a pleasant mountain road, the next highlight was Shuswap Lake, a huge lake surrounding the town of Salmon Arm. Parts of this lake were frozen and parts weren't. We had seen many completely frozen white lakes before, but this was the first time in Canada we had seen a lake of jewel-like blue water surrounded by white snowy mountains.

With the Thompson River, which flows out of Shuswap Lake, on our right, we followed the river and reached the city of Kamloops, which we had passed through on day 6 on the way from Squamish to Jasper. We had lunch at a restaurant in this city.

From Kamloops we headed south on Highway 5, the Yellowhead Highway. It's a divided highway and easy to drive, but we saw two cars that had been in rear-end collisions. We couldn't relax until Vancouver. For a while there are few towns along the road, and places to refuel are limited. We left the highway briefly to refuel at a town called Hope. Big lumps of muddy snow were stuck around the car's wheels. While refuelling we cleaned off the dirt too.

While refuelling at the station in Hope, something went wrong with the Jeep. A mysterious liquid sprayed out of the engine bay like a mist. On top of that, while idling, the coolant temperature rose and the gauge pointed at H. The cooling fan had broken in the collision, so the radiator probably couldn't cool unless the car was moving. Very worried, we set off again. After driving for a while the temperature came down, but this time an abnormal metallic scraping noise came from around the wheels. We stopped the car once, but couldn't tell where the problem was. 150 km to Vancouver. All we could do was pray it would make it today. We went back on the highway and kept driving. The metallic noise continued, but gradually got quieter until we stopped noticing it. Maybe the parts had worn themselves smooth.
Around Abbotsford, about 60 km before Vancouver, the feel of the city begins. Just 5 km south of here is Washington State in America. The far part of the view is probably America.

On the roads around here we saw lots of crashed cars. Rollovers, collisions, cars off the road, pile-ups; we lost count. On monotonous roads with many straights, falling asleep may be the main cause. Or maybe it's because places that would have an 80 km/h limit on a Japanese expressway almost all have a 100 km/h limit here.

Before Vancouver we were caught in a traffic jam for a while. The night view in the distance was beautiful. Vancouver was close. But we still hadn't decided where to stay tonight either. From experience so far, we thought we'd soon find a motel. We entered Vancouver and looked for somewhere to stay. But we couldn't find anything. The Days Inn we finally found after searching and searching was fully booked. In the end we stayed at the Cambie Hostel, which we had listed in our trip plan. First, there was no car park. We didn't want to park on the street, so we reluctantly used a coin car park.

It was cheap, but the room was small and shabby, with just simple bunk beds. For now we went to get dinner. The ground floor of the Cambie Hostel is a pub, so we ate there. But the music was far too loud. You could barely hear each other talk. Even when sleeping in the room, the noise from downstairs echoed up until late at night.
□ Day 16 (27 Feb) Vancouver (stay)
Today was a completely free day until the evening's farewell party. We spent the whole day seeing the sights of Vancouver. Let me introduce the places the four of us visited.
Right near the Cambie Hostel is Gastown. An old district whose symbol is the steam clock.

The building jutting into the inlet, with four sails as its symbol, is Canada Place. The view from the deck-like area of the buildings along the downtown waterfront and the opposite shore of the inlet is superb.
Robson Street: the main street in the middle of downtown, lined with all kinds of shops. Canadian specialities, brand-name shops; window shopping alone is plenty of fun.

The coast on the south-west side of downtown is called English Bay Beach, and a very beautiful sandy beach stretches along it. There are lawns and promenades, and lots of locals jogging, walking dogs and roller-skating. Go a little way into town and it's a big city of high-rise buildings, but the atmosphere here is calm and pleasant. The sea water is surprisingly clean and clear. Ducks and seabirds gather in flocks and rest on the water. Especially recommended when you're tired of the city atmosphere.

On a small peninsula in False Creek, an inlet south of downtown, is Granville Island, a large shopping area. Lined with markets and food courts, it seemed busy not only with tourists but locals too. The square was full of all kinds of birds, after food. Tear off some bread and give it to them, and the birds all rush at you at once.

City buses are handy for getting around Vancouver. $2.50 to anywhere in the city. Once you buy a ticket, you can transfer freely for 90 minutes. A day pass sells for $9. There are plenty of services and routes, but there are too many stops; they stop almost every block. Maybe not for people in a hurry.
A little way from downtown is the University of British Columbia, the largest university in western Canada, so big it's practically a university town.

Taking the boat called the SeaBus, you can go to the city of North Vancouver, north of Vancouver. The fare is $3.75, and you can ride with a city bus day pass too. Getting off the SeaBus, right beside it is Lonsdale Quay Market, which we failed to reach on day 1. Granville Island had all sorts of shops outdoors, while Lonsdale Quay Market had various shops inside a big building.

In the evening we met up, and before the farewell party we went to the Lookout observation deck in a high-rise called Harbour Centre. It's the fourth-tallest building in Vancouver, with a 360° view. And since it was night, we could see a superb night view. By the way, on this page you can experience the daytime and evening views from the Lookout. (Vancouver Lookout official website)

And then the farewell party, at a brewpub called Steamworks. Our 16 days in Canada felt like they had flown by. At one point we worried we might not be able to get back to Japan, but we had made it safely back to Vancouver, and now we only had to start for home tomorrow. Enjoying delicious local beer brewed at the brewpub and good food, and sharing memories, the Vancouver night wore on.
□ Day 17 (28 Feb) Vancouver → Air Canada AC001

At last the time came to return to Japan. First we went to the Jeep, which had worked so hard with us. The total charge for the coin car park reached $42. A bigger expense than expected. The last run to the airport. A final refuel at a petrol station before Vancouver International Airport. We wanted to give it a wash, but there was no car wash, so we couldn't.

Then we arrived at the Alamo rent-a-car lot. As we unloaded the bags, a staff member came over. We showed him the broken bumper. And seeing it, he said: "No problem!!" Wow, generous. We weren't charged an accident excess either, and the return was completed without any trouble. Jeep Grand Cherokee, thank you for all your hard work. The final total distance was 6,304 km.

We checked in, cleared baggage checks, had breakfast, spent time shopping in the duty-free area until boarding, and got on the plane at about 1 p.m. The flight home was about nine and a half hours. Because we were chasing the sun, it stayed overhead the whole time until about 15:30 on 1 March, Japan time. The weather was good, and over Alaska we could see Mt. McKinley below.
□ Day 18 (1 Mar) Air Canada AC001 → Tokyo

We crossed the date line and it became 1 March. The plane passed over the base of the Kamchatka Peninsula, Sakhalin, Hokkaido and the Sanriku coast. The Sea of Okhotsk was covered in drift ice, and we could clearly see Sakhalin's snowy mountains and wide plains from the window. Then we landed at Narita Airport. Japan, for the first time in a while. Seeing so much Japanese writing was a relief.

We had plenty of time until the night bus from Tokyo Station, so we killed time at the airport, using the internet on a laptop and napping. I think we were pretty tired. After that we went to JR and boarded the night bus.
□ Day 19 (2 Mar) Tokyo → Nagoya

When I woke up we were already at the west side of Nagoya Station. Wow, how nostalgic. Getting off the bus, the first thing that caught my eye was a Yoshinoya sign. Come to think of it, there were many Japanese restaurants in Canada, but I don't think there was any gyudon. The trip ended with a Yoshinoya beef bowl. It really sank in that we were back in Japan.
— The End —
